title: Annotation on the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings
author: Zhanran
excerpt: This sutra sets out to explain the eight dharmas to which the bodhisattva (the "great being" of the sutra) awakens: the realization of impermanence and non-self, the realization of few desires and non-doing, the realization of contentment in poverty and guarding the Way, the realization of constant diligence, the realization of much learning and growing wisdom, the realization of equal regard for enemies and kin, the realization of the harms of the five desires, and the realization of the great mind that universally aids all — so as to accomplish self-awakening and the awakening of others.

inline.s: Course
Textbook

This sutra sets out to explain the eight dharmas to which the bodhisattva (the "great being" of the sutra) awakens: the realization of impermanence and non-self, the realization of few desires and non-doing, the realization of contentment in poverty and guarding the Way, the realization of constant diligence, the realization of much learning and growing wisdom, the realization of equal regard for enemies and kin, the realization of the harms of the five desires, and the realization of the great mind that universally aids all — so as to accomplish self-awakening and the awakening of others.
Note: for ease of understanding and reference, each passage is prefixed with a number and a heading; these are not part of the sutra text.
[The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings]

In the title, "the eight realizations of the great beings" means the eight dharmas that the bodhisattva constantly reflects upon and awakens to. A "great being" is a person of great power; here it refers to the bodhisattva.
[Translated by the Eastern Han śramaṇa An Shigao]

śramaṇa,” translated into Chinese as "diligent rest," means diligent effort in the Buddha-way and the stilling of all afflictions; it is the general term for one who has left home to cultivate the Way. An Shigao was a great monk of the Han era, originally the crown prince of the kingdom of Parthia (present-day Iran), named An Qing, styled Shigao. When his father the king died, he succeeded to the throne. But weary of the world, he yielded the throne to his uncle, left home to study the Way, and was widely versed in the teachings of the three vehicles. He then travelled through many lands, spreading the Buddha-dharma. In the second year of Jianhe (A.D.

), he came to Luoyang. He first studied the Chinese language, and then translated Buddhist scriptures — in all as many as twenty-nine sutras and treatises. An Shigao's work of translation ended about the Jianning era of the Eastern Han (
). Thereafter he travelled through Jiangxi, Zhejiang, and other places. Quite a number of marvelous stories about him circulate among the people.
The three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the bodhisattva.
[Being disciples of the Buddha, always by day and by night, with utmost sincerity, recite and contemplate the eight realizations of the great beings.]

As disciples of the Buddha, we should always, by day and by night, with utmost sincerity recite, contemplate, and cultivate the eight realizations of the bodhisattva: the realization of impermanence and non-self, the realization of few desires and non-doing, the realization of contentment in poverty and guarding the Way, the realization of constant diligence, the realization of much learning and growing wisdom, the realization of equal regard for enemies and kin, the realization of the harms of the five desires, and the realization of the great mind that universally aids all.

always by day and by night,” means that the practice is unbroken. "With utmost sincerity" means genuine and single-minded. "Recite and contemplate" means one should be thoroughly familiar with the meaning, keep it engraved upon the heart, and always reflect upon it, checking oneself against it.
Disciples of the Buddha: whether at home or having left home, as long as one takes refuge in the Buddha, one is a disciple of the Buddha.

Always reflecting and checking oneself against it: this is the method of calm and insight — stilling the deluded thoughts that arise from worldly thoughts, keeping the inner mind calm and steady, so as to gather the mind and observe and contemplate the eight realizations of the great beings, reaching the state of wisdom. Calm and insight: "calm" means stilling deluded thoughts and concentrating the mind on a single point; it is the foundation of "insight." With the work of calm, insight can be focused, deep, and sustained. "Insight" means observing the truth and thoroughly transforming the erroneous views and standpoints latent in the subconscious, turning from the views of an ordinary being to the views of the Buddha. In this whole process of steeping practice, utmost sincerity and unbrokenness are very important. Calm and insight are the two wheels of the vehicle traveling upon the bodhi path; neither can be lacking. To be calm without insight is to have concentration without wisdom; to be insightful without calm, the wisdom is hard to achieve.
Question: How does one practice calm (śamatha)?

Answer: There are many methods for practicing calm. For example, the "preliminary practice" portion of the actual-practice lesson "Awareness and Recitation of the Buddha" in the Shuoxiuxing Online Buddhist Academy's program is itself the practice of calm.

[First, awaken to the impermanence of the world, and that the land is fragile and perilous. The four elements are suffering and empty; the five aggregates are without self. Rising and ceasing, changing and transforming, they are false and without a master. The mind is the source of evil; the body is the gathering-place of offenses. Observing thus, one gradually departs from birth and death.]

First, awaken to the impermanence of the world and that the land is fragile and perilous. The material body (the four elements) is both suffering and empty; the body and mind (the five aggregates) are without self. They rise and cease, change and transform; they are false and without a master. The mind is the source of all evil; the body is the place where all offenses gather. Observing thus, one gradually departs from birth and death.
The first contemplation is to awaken to the environment and to the "self."

"Contemplate" means to visualize and reflect in accord with principle; "observe" (investigate) means to see through, to verify. So it is not only to think of it often and recite it often, but also to realize it in one's own being and to practice it.
Contemplating the environment:
awaken to the impermanence of the world and the fragility of the land

" — everything in the world is changing and impermanent, like a revolving-picture lantern, like a kaleidoscope; and the land is perilous and fragile as well, often beset by foreign invasion or internal disorder, and by the many different natural disasters.

This first contemplates the defiled and evil nature of the environment in which we live: not only is there nothing to rely upon or cling to, but one should make haste to depart from it. The Essential Instructions on Cultivating the Mind says: "The three realms are hot and troubled, like a burning house; can you bear to linger on, willingly receiving endless suffering?"
Contemplating the so-called "self (body and mind)"

the four elements are suffering and empty, the five aggregates are without self; rising and ceasing, changing and transforming, they are false and without a master; the mind is the source of evil, the body the gathering-place of offenses

" — to awaken that the material body (the four elements) is suffering and illusory, that the body and mind (the five aggregates) are not my self; that the body and mind falsely dress themselves up as "me," and yet cannot be the master of their own birth, aging, sickness, and death, their pain and sorrow (rising, ceasing, changing, transforming); and moreover that
the mind is the source of all evil and the body the gathering-place of all offenses

The body is composed of the four elements (earth, water, fire, wind); when a person dies the four elements separate, so how can there still be a body? Without a body, naturally there are no six faculties; without the six faculties one does not contact the six objects; and since there is no contact with the six objects, how can there be feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (the mind)? With neither body nor mind, how can there be a self? How can there be a world? Therefore all things are empty.

The reason sentient beings chase after objects, produce karma, and transmigrate in birth and death is precisely that they falsely cling to body, mind, and world as real existents, and take body and mind to be themselves. Therefore, the first thing to do is to break through the view of self.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of upside-down views, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four elements as the mark of the self-body, and the shadow-images of the six objects as the mark of the self-mind. It is like one whose eyes are diseased, seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In the sky there are in truth no flowers; it is the diseased one that falsely clings. Because of this false clinging, not only is he deluded about the empty nature of the sky, but he is also deluded about where the real flowers come from. Because of this, falsely there is turning in birth and death; this is called ignorance."

The Essential Instructions on Cultivating the Mind says: "The hundred bones dissolve, returning to fire and returning to wind; the one thing ever numinous (intrinsic nature) covers heaven and covers the earth." Therefore one must not falsely cling to the body as self; rather, one must let the ever-numinous master take charge. This is the key to escaping birth and death.

The four elements: the element of earth, the element of water, the element of fire, and the element of wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has wetness as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. All the formed matter of the world has the four natures of solidity, wetness, warmth, and movement; hence they are called "elements." For example, the hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, sinews, and flesh of the human body are the earth element of solid nature; saliva, phlegm, pus, blood, spittle, tears, urine, and excrement are the water element of wet nature; warmth and heat are the fire element of warm nature; and each inhalation and exhalation is the wind element of moving nature. Likewise, the trunks and branches of plants are the earth element of solid nature; the moisture within them is the water element of wet nature; drawing up the nutrients of the soil in order to grow is the fire element of warm nature; and absorbing carbon dioxide and emitting oxygen is the wind element of moving nature. The six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The eye is the faculty of sight, the ear the faculty of hearing, the nose the faculty of smell, the tongue the faculty of taste, the body the faculty of touch, and the mind the faculty of thought. "Faculty" has the meaning of being able to generate, just as a plant with roots can produce trunk and branches. The six objects: the object of form, of sound, of smell, of taste, of touch, and of mental objects. "Object" has the meaning of defiling — they are able to defile people's pure minds, so that true nature cannot reveal itself. They are also called the six fields, the external objects in dependence upon which the six faculties arise. The shadow-images of the six objects: the various thoughts produced when the six faculties reach the six objects; and since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadow-images of the six objects — the illusory reflections of the six objects.

The five aggregates: that is, the "five skandhas," form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness — the five great elements constituting body and mind; form is the physical body, while feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the mind. Because they accumulate and arise, they are called "skandhas" (aggregates); and because they can cover over a person's true nature, causing confusion and upside-downness and the making of all sorts of karma, they are also called the "five covers." The five aggregates without self: the body and mind of a person are but a temporary union of the five aggregates; when the conditions gather they arise, when the conditions scatter they cease; there is no unchanging self-substance. False and without a master: "self" has the meaning of mastery; yet the body and mind are quite unable to be master over their own rising and ceasing, changing and transforming, and over the stirring of delusion and the making of karma. Hence they are said to be false and without a master. A gathering-place of offenses: the deep pool of evil. A "deep pool" is the place where fish and beasts gather; it is also used as a metaphor for the place where certain persons or things gather. A marsh (
sou
): a lake-marsh in which many grasses grow.
observing thus, one gradually departs from birth and death
" — contemplate, reflect, and see through it in this way, and at all times check whether one has truly awakened to it; doing so, one may gradually depart from birth and death.
[Second, awaken to the realization that many desires are suffering. The weariness of birth and death arises from greed and desire; with few desires and non-doing, body and mind are at ease.]

Second: one must always awaken to the root of suffering that is many desires. Birth and death and weariness and toil all arise from greed and desire; therefore one should have few desires and practice non-doing, so as to make body and mind at ease.
Body and mind at ease — this is the prerequisite for cultivating the Way. If all day long one is anxiously seeking and busily scheming, restless and uneasy, how can one practice the Way?

The evil karmas done in the past all arise from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, produced through body, speech, and mind.” Evil karma is made by body, speech, and mind, and body, speech, and mind are in turn driven by greed, hatred, and delusion. Among greed, hatred, and delusion, greed is the root. When greed is not satisfied there is hatred; greed and hatred cloud clear reason, so that one thinks, speaks, and acts against principle — this is delusion. From this it can be seen that greed is the source of all evil, and that desire is in turn the driving force of greed. If one would cultivate the Way, the first thing is to leave desire behind.

The first realization before was to subdue the delusions of views; now the second realization is to subdue the delusions of thought. Though the delusions of thought are many, greed and desire lead them. If one can practice few desires, then one can awaken to non-doing and attain ease!

The delusions of views and the delusions of thought: the delusions of views are the confusions and errors of ordinary beings in their views, such as the five wrong views — the view of self, the view of extremes, the wrong view, the view holding to views, and the view holding to precepts and practices. The delusions of thought are the confusions and errors of ordinary beings in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of sentient beings' drifting in the three realms and vainly enduring birth and death; cutting them off, one can end birth and death and leave the three realms. The weariness of birth and death arising from greed and desire: greed and desire are not only the root of weariness, but also the root of the revolution of birth and death, so the cultivation of the Way must sever greed and desire. The five views, also called the five wrong views: the view of self, the view of extremes, the wrong view, the view holding to views, and the view holding to precepts and practices. The view of self is clinging to the temporarily-united body of the five aggregates as a real existent; the view of extremes is an evil view that leans to one side — for example, some hold that after death everything returns to nothing, the so-called death is like a lamp going out, and this is called the view of annihilation, while others hold that after death a person is still a person, and that pigs, horses, cattle, and sheep remain pigs, horses, cattle, and sheep, and this is called the view of eternalism; such views, clinging to annihilation or to eternalism, all lean to one side, hence they are called views of extremes. The wrong view is a wicked and not-right view, such as denying cause and effect or destroying good works. The view holding to views is holding the above views of self, extremes, and wrong to be right. The view holding to precepts and practices is the practice or undertaking of wrong precepts, mistaking them for right ones — for example, some hold to the ox-precept and the dog-precept, thinking this to be the cause of rebirth in heaven, while others smear ash and fast, mistaking it for the way of nirvāṇa. Smearing ash: smearing ash over the whole body and seeking rebirth in heaven through ascetic practices.

blocks.text: 3. Content in Poverty, Guarding the Way

inline.s: [Third, awaken to the realization that the mind is never satiated, and that simply to gain and seek much only increases wrongdoing. The bodhisattva is not so; he always thinks of contentment, is content in poverty and guards the Way, and makes wisdom alone his work.]

Third: one must always awaken to the fact that the habitual nature of the mind is never satisfied, and that simply taking obtaining and seeking much as one's occupation results in growing wrongdoing. The bodhisattva is not like this; he is always few in desires and content, content in poverty and guarding the Way, taking the growth of wisdom alone as his work.

Wisdom: the wisdom that is not confused or turned upside down and thoroughly knows the true nature of all dharmas; this is the prajñā among the six perfections. To make wisdom alone one's work: here "work" means one's occupation (the things one engages in and practices). The six perfections: the six kinds of practice that can ferry one from the shore of birth-and-death suffering to the shore of nirvāṇa's peace and bliss, namely giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and prajñā.

[Fourth, awaken to the realization that indolence causes one to fall. Practice constant diligence, break through the evil of affliction, subdue the four maras, and step out of the prison of the aggregates and elements.]

Fourth: one must always awaken to the fact that indolence makes one fall. Therefore one must practice constant diligence, break through the evil habits of affliction, subdue the four maras (the mara of affliction, the mara of the aggregates, the mara of death, and the mara of the heavens), and step out of the prison constituted by the five aggregates and the eighteen elements (ending birth and death, and leaving the three realms).

The four maras: the mara of affliction, the mara of the aggregates, the mara of death, and the mara of the heavens. The mara of affliction refers to such habits as greed, hatred, and delusion, which can harry the body and mind; the mara of the aggregates refers to such aggregates as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which give rise to all suffering; the mara of death refers to death, which can cut off a person's life-root; the mara of the heavens is mara Pāpīyas, the king of the sixth heaven of the realm of desire, who has a countless retinue and constantly obstructs the Buddha-way. The prison of the aggregates and elements: "aggregates and elements" refers to the five aggregates and the eighteen elements; "the prison of the aggregates and elements" is the prison formed by the five aggregates and the eighteen elements. The eighteen elements: the general name for the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), the six objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects), and the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness). The three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world where beings still bound by the two desires of lust and appetite dwell, from the six heavens of desire above, through the dusty world of humans and animals, down to the hungry ghosts and hells; the realm of form is the heaven-world of beings free of the two desires of lust and appetite but still having bodily forms; the formless realm is the heaven-world of beings who have neither form but rest their mind-consciousness in deep and subtle meditative concentration. These three realms are the states in which ordinary beings come and go through birth and death, and so the Buddhist practitioner aims to leap out of the three realms.

[Fifth, awaken to the realization that ignorance is birth and death. The bodhisattva constantly thinks to study broadly and hear much, to grow in wisdom, to accomplish eloquence, and to teach and transform all, all with great joy.]

Fifth, awaken to the fact that ignorance (non-awakening) leads to birth and death. Therefore, the bodhisattva constantly thinks to study broadly and hear much, so as to grow in wisdom and be no longer ignorant, to accomplish eloquence, and to teach and transform all sentient beings, saving them as much as possible with great joy (the ending of birth and death).

Awakening to the fact that ignorance is birth and death: to awaken that ignorance leads to birth and death. "Ignorance (non-awakening)" is to be confused and upside-down, falsely clinging to body and mind as real and as self, and so chasing after objects and producing karma, receiving retribution according to one's karma, and transmigrating endlessly in birth and death. To awaken that ignorance leads to the revolution of birth and death, one should study broadly and hear much, increase wisdom (no longer be ignorant), awaken oneself and awaken others, save oneself and save others. Ignorance: here ignorance means non-awakening. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "What is ignorance? Good man! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of upside-down views, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions for one another (for example, taking east for west, south for north, and so on), falsely taking the four elements as the mark of the self-body, and the shadow-images of the six objects as the mark of the self-mind. It is like one whose eyes are diseased, seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In the sky there are in truth no flowers; it is the diseased one that falsely clings. Because of this false clinging, not only is he deluded about the empty nature of the sky, but he is also deluded about where the real flowers come from. Because of this, falsely there is turning in birth and death; this is called ignorance."

blocks.text: 6. Equal Regard for Enemies and Kin

inline.s: [Sixth, awaken to the realization that poverty and suffering bring much resentment, and that one thereby crosses into bad karmic ties. When the bodhisattva gives, he regards enemies and kin alike, does not remember past wrongs, and does not hate evil men.]

Sixth: one must always awaken to the fact that if one takes poverty as suffering there is much resentment, and one will cross over into bad karmic ties and bring calamity and retribution upon oneself; therefore one should be content in poverty and delight in the Way. When the bodhisattva gives, he should regard enemies and kin with the same care, not remembering past wrongs, and not hating wicked people.

blocks.text: 7. The Harms of the Five Desires

inline.s: [Seventh, awaken to the harms of the five desires, and, though a lay person, do not be stained by worldly pleasures. Always think of the three robes, the clay bowl, and the ritual implements; resolve to leave home, guard the Way in purity, keep an exalted and far-reaching pure conduct, and be compassionate to all.]

Seventh, awaken to the harms of the five desires; though one is a householder, one should not be stained by the pleasures of the world. Always think that one is a śramaṇa holding the three robes, the clay bowl, and the ritual implements, and vow to leave home; therefore one should guard the Way in purity, keep pure conduct exalted and far-reaching, and pour compassion over all sentient beings.

The five desires: form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearance; sound refers to pleasing voices and delightful words; smell refers to fragrant scents; taste refers to delicious flavors; touch refers to agreeable tactile pleasures. These five, because they can cause people to produce greedy minds, are called the five desires. To keep the precepts pure is to be able to control the five faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) and not be moved by the five desires. The three robes: the antarvāsa, the uttarāsaṅga, and the saṃghāṭī. The antarvāsa is translated as the under-robe, made of five strips, and is worn in ordinary daily life and sleep; the uttarāsaṅga is translated as the upper-robe, made of seven strips, and is worn on going into the assembly for ceremonies; the saṃghāṭī is translated as the robe of the gathered assembly, again called the great robe, made of from nine to twenty-five strips, and is worn at great assemblies, or when seeing the head of state or high ministers. Pure conduct: pure and clean practice. One who cultivates pure conduct may, after death, be born in the brahma heavens.

blocks.text: 8. The Great Mind That Universally Aids

inline.s: [Eighth, awaken to the realization that birth and death blaze fiercely, and that suffering and distress are measureless. Put forth the mind of the Great Vehicle, universally succor all, be willing to take upon oneself the measureless suffering of sentient beings, and cause them all to reach final great joy.]

Eighth: one must always awaken to the fact that from birth to death a person is as if roasting in a great fire, with measureless suffering and distress. Therefore one should put forth the mind of the Great Vehicle, universally save all sentient beings, be willing to take upon oneself the measureless suffering of sentient beings, and cause them all finally to attain the great joy of ending birth and death.

The mind of the Great Vehicle: one who possesses the bodhi mind, the mind of great compassion, and the mind of skillful means is said to have the "mind of the Great Vehicle." The Vimalakīrti Sutra says: "The mind of the Great Vehicle is the bodhisattva's Pure Land." The mind of skillful means: the mind that saves sentient beings by means of various skills. Skillful means: the devices, methods, or language employed to guide and teach sentient beings.

[These eight matters are what the great beings, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, have awakened to. Diligently practice the Way, cultivate wisdom with compassion, ride the ship of the dharmakāya, and reach the shore of nirvāṇa; then return again to birth and death to deliver sentient beings.]

These eight matters are the wonderful dharmas to which the great beings (persons of great power), the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, have awakened. One should always remember them and diligently practice the Way, cultivate wisdom with compassion, ride the precious ship of the dharmakāya, and go straight on to the shore of nirvāṇa; then, turning the ship of compassion back around, one returns again to the realm of birth and death (the sahā world) to deliver sentient beings.

The three bodies: the Buddha has three bodies — the dharmakāya, the saṃbhogakāya, and the nirmāṇakāya. The dharmakāya, also called the body of intrinsic nature or the body of the nature of dharmas, is the eternal, undying true nature originally possessed by everyone; only in us sentient beings the dharmakāya is present but deluded and not manifest, whereas the Buddha has awakened and realized it. The saṃbhogakāya is formed by the Buddha's wisdom and merit. It has a self-enjoyment body and an other-enjoyment body: the self-enjoyment body is the body by which the Buddha himself enjoys the dharma-bliss of inner realization; the other-enjoyment body is the body manifested by the Buddha to preach the Dharma for the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The nirmāṇakāya, also called the transformation body or the emanation body, is the Buddha-body manifested in response to the karmic opportunities of sentient beings.

Nirvāṇa: translated into Chinese as "perfect quiescence," perfect being the full perfection of all wisdom and virtue, and quiescence the quelling of all delusion and karma. It is also translated as "crossing over through extinction," extinction being the removal of the three delusions of views and thought, of dust-sand, and of ignorance, and crossing over being the deliverance from the two kinds of birth and death, the intermittent and the transformation. Combined, it means that when a person's wisdom and virtue have both reached the utterly perfect realm, and even birth and death and affliction have been transcended and forever cut off, this is called "nirvāṇa." It is also the realm of true thusness realized by the sages, unborn and undying, transcending time and space; and it is the most ideal and most beautiful final destination of the teeming multitudes of beings.

The birth and death of the intermittent body: all sentient beings, within the three realms and six destinies, because of the retribution of good and evil karma, have their life spans limited and their bodies in sections; hence their birth and death is called "the birth and death of the intermittent body." The birth and death of transformation: the sages among the three vehicles (the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the bodhisattva) have cut off the delusions of views and thought and ended the birth and death of the intermittent body. But because of the result of their cultivation, deluded thinking gradually ceases and realization gradually grows; this transition of delusion and awakening differs in each stage, and the moving from an earlier stage into a later one is like a passing through birth and death, whose transformation is mysterious and unfathomable and beyond thought; hence it is called "the birth and death of transformation," or "the inconceivable birth and death of transformation." Returning to birth and death: the bodhisattva, having realized the Way, has ended birth and death, and turning the ship of compassion back around, returns again to the sahā world to save sentient beings, and so will pass through birth and death again; hence it is said "returning to birth and death." Yet though the bodhisattva enters birth and death, he is able to be master and at ease; whereas ordinary beings are bound and pressed by birth and death.
[With these eight matters, guide all beings, causing them to awaken to the suffering of birth and death, to abandon the five desires, and to cultivate the mind in the holy Way.]

One should use the eight matters expounded above to guide all sentient beings, causing them to awaken to the suffering of birth and death, abandon the five desires, and single-mindedly cultivate the eightfold noble path.

The eightfold noble path: that is, the eight dharmas of the noble ones. First, right view — correct views and understanding. Second, right thought — correct thinking. Third, right speech — proper speech. Fourth, right action — proper action. Fifth, right livelihood — proper means of livelihood or living. Sixth, right effort — proper effort. Seventh, right mindfulness — correct mindfulness. Eighth, right concentration — correct meditative concentration.

[If disciples of the Buddha recite these eight matters, in thought after thought they extinguish measureless offenses; advancing toward bodhi, they quickly mount to right enlightenment, forever cut off birth and death, and dwell forever in happiness.]

If disciples of the Buddha, with utmost sincerity, recite and contemplate these eight matters, in thought after thought they extinguish measureless offenses; by this, advancing bravely upon the bodhi path, they quickly become Buddhas, forever cut off birth and death, and dwell forever in happiness.
Advancing toward bodhi: that is, moving toward bodhi; "toward" means advancing toward. Quickly mounting to right enlightenment: quickly becoming a Buddha.
